sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 94 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: The Judge of the earth
study.intro: Psalm 94 cries out to God as Judge when the powerful crush the weak. It rebukes those who think God does not see, blesses those He disciplines and teaches, and ends in the psalmist's personal testimony that the LORD held him up and is his rock of refuge.
study.context: Psalm 94 has no heading in the Hebrew text. It sits among the 'LORD reigns' psalms of Book IV, reminding readers that the King is also the Judge. Verses 1-7 appeal against corrupt oppressors who harm widows, foreigners and orphans; verses 8-15 rebuke fools and bless the disciplined; verses 16-23 give personal testimony of God's help. Jewish tradition sang it on the fourth day of the week.
study.peopleNote: No author is named. Jacob is linked because the oppressors mock 'the God of Jacob.' Jesus is linked as the Judge who sees the hidden thoughts of every heart. God is never portrayed as a human body in planned art.

verses.title: God of vengeance
verses.heading: Shine forth
verses.meaning: The psalm opens with a bold cry: 'O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth.' Vengeance here is not petty revenge but God's just repayment of evil. When the powerful abuse others and no human court stops them, the only hope is the Judge of all. 'Shine forth' asks God to appear in brightness, as He did at Sinai, and make His justice visible.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 32:35 records God saying, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.' Romans 12:19 quotes this to tell believers not to avenge themselves. Psalm 50:2 says, 'From Zion, perfect in beauty, God shines forth.'
explore: Vengeance
God's rightful, just repayment of wrongdoing, not personal spite or revenge.
Shine forth
To appear in brilliant light, a picture of God revealing Himself in power.
verses.reflect: What injustice do you need to bring to God rather than trying to settle yourself?
verses.alt: Bright sunlight bursts through dark clouds over a quiet town.

verses.title: Rise up, O Judge
verses.heading: Repaying the proud
verses.meaning: Verse 2 continues, 'Rise up, O Judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud.' God is pictured as a judge who seems to be sitting quietly, and the psalmist asks Him to stand and act. The 'reward' is what the proud deserve. Arrogance assumes no one is above it, but there is a Judge over the whole earth, and He will give everyone what is due.
verses.context: Genesis 18:25 records Abraham asking, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Proverbs 16:18 says pride goes before destruction. Acts 17:31 says God has set a day to judge the world through the Man He appointed.
explore: Judge of the earth
God as the supreme ruler who decides justly for all nations and people.
The proud
Those who exalt themselves and act as if they answer to no one, including God.
verses.reflect: Is there pride in your own heart that needs to be humbled before the Judge?
verses.alt: An empty stone judgment seat sits at a city gate at dawn.

verses.title: How long?
verses.heading: Wicked people exult
verses.meaning: Verse 3 asks the age-old question: 'How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?' The doubled 'how long' shows the strain of waiting. Evildoers celebrate their success while the faithful suffer. Scripture does not forbid this question; it gives words for it. Bringing our impatience honestly to God is itself an act of faith, because we still address Him.
verses.context: Psalm 13:1 asks, 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?' Habakkuk 1:2 cries, 'How long, O LORD, must I call for help?' Revelation 6:10 records the martyrs asking, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true?'
explore: Exult
To rejoice triumphantly or gloat, often over others' misfortune.
How long
A cry of lament asking God when He will finally act against evil.
verses.reflect: What 'how long' question do you need to bring honestly to God?
verses.alt: A lone figure waits on a rooftop watching a long empty road.

verses.title: Arrogant words
verses.heading: Boasting workers of iniquity
verses.meaning: Verse 4 describes the wicked: 'They pour out arrogant words; all workers of iniquity boast.' Their speech flows nonstop like water from a spring. Boasting reveals what fills their hearts: pride and contempt. Words are not harmless; they shape how others are treated. The psalmist notes that evil often begins with arrogant talk long before it becomes violent action.
verses.context: Proverbs 18:21 says death and life are in the power of the tongue. James 3:5-6 compares the tongue to a small fire that sets a forest ablaze. Matthew 12:34 records Jesus saying the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart.
explore: Iniquity
Wickedness or sin, especially deliberate wrongdoing that twists what is right.
Boast
To speak proudly about oneself, claiming power or credit to impress others.
verses.reflect: What do your words this week reveal about the condition of your heart?
verses.alt: Men argue loudly in a busy ancient marketplace under awnings.

verses.title: Crushing Your people
verses.heading: Oppressing Your heritage
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says, 'They crush Your people, O LORD; they oppress Your heritage.' The psalmist reminds God that the victims belong to Him. Israel is His heritage, His treasured possession. To harm them is to attack what God loves. This gives the prayer its force: God's own honor is involved when His people are crushed. He will not ignore what is done to His own.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 32:9 says, 'The LORD's portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance.' Zechariah 2:8 says whoever touches God's people touches the apple of His eye. Acts 9:4 records Jesus asking Saul, 'Why do you persecute Me?'
explore: Heritage
An inheritance or treasured possession; here God's people, who belong to Him.
Oppress
To keep people down by cruel or unjust use of power and authority.
verses.reflect: How does knowing you belong to God change how you face mistreatment?
verses.alt: Laborers bend under heavy loads in a dusty brickyard.

verses.title: Widow and foreigner
verses.heading: Preying on the vulnerable
verses.meaning: Verse 6 names the victims: 'They kill the widow and the foreigner; they murder the fatherless.' These were the most defenseless people in ancient society, with no husband, land or family to protect them. God's law specially guarded them. Those who prey on them commit a particularly evil crime. God's heart is always for the weak, and He expects His people to share it.
verses.context: Exodus 22:22 commands, 'You must not mistreat any widow or orphan.' Deuteronomy 10:18 says God executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner. James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows.
explore: Fatherless
Children without fathers, who in ancient times often lacked protection and provision.
Foreigner
A non-Israelite living in Israel, often without land, family or legal power.
verses.reflect: Who are the vulnerable people near you whom God may be asking you to protect?
verses.alt: A widow and her small children sit beside a simple doorway.

verses.title: The LORD does not see
verses.heading: Mocking the God of Jacob
verses.meaning: Verse 7 exposes the oppressors' belief: 'They say, The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed.' Their cruelty grows from a lie, that God is blind or uninterested. Practical atheism says God may exist, but He does not notice or care. Mentioning 'the God of Jacob' is ironic: He is the God who saw Jacob in every trouble and kept His promises.
verses.context: Genesis 16:13 records Hagar calling God 'the God who sees me.' Genesis 28:15 records God promising Jacob, 'I am with you and will watch over you.' Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight.
explore: God of Jacob
A title recalling God's faithful care for Jacob and his descendants, Israel.
Pays no heed
Does not pay attention or care about what is happening.
verses.reflect: Do you ever act as though God does not see? How would remembering He sees change you?
verses.alt: Two schemers whisper in a shadowed alley beside clay jars.

verses.title: When will you be wise?
verses.heading: A warning to fools
verses.meaning: Verse 8 turns to address the wrongdoers and those tempted to follow them: 'Take notice, O senseless among the people! O fools, when will you be wise?' The psalmist pleads rather than just condemns. Even foolish people can still learn. The question 'when' implies there is still time to change. God's warnings are invitations to wisdom before judgment arrives.
verses.context: Proverbs 1:22 asks, 'How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways?' Proverbs 9:10 says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Ephesians 5:15 urges believers to walk not as unwise but as wise.
explore: Senseless
Brutish or dull, lacking spiritual understanding and acting without thought.
Wise
Having understanding that leads to right living, beginning with reverence for God.
verses.reflect: Is there a warning you have been ignoring that God wants you to take seriously?
verses.alt: A teacher points to an open scroll before seated young men.

verses.title: He who formed the eye
verses.heading: Can He not see?
verses.meaning: Verse 9 offers a sharp argument: 'He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?' The One who designed hearing and sight must Himself hear and see perfectly. It is absurd to think the Creator is less aware than His creatures. Every ear and eye testifies to a Maker who notices everything, including hidden injustice.
verses.context: Exodus 4:11 records God asking Moses, 'Who gave man his mouth? ... Is it not I, the LORD?' Proverbs 20:12 says the hearing ear and seeing eye were both made by the LORD. Psalm 139:13 praises God for forming us.
explore: Affixed
Fastened in place; here God planting the ear in the human body.
Formed
Shaped or fashioned with skill, as a potter shapes clay.
verses.reflect: How does the design of your own body remind you that God sees and hears you?
verses.alt: A potter's hands carefully shape soft clay on a turning wheel.

verses.title: Teacher of nations
verses.heading: Does He not discipline?
verses.meaning: Verse 10 continues the reasoning: 'He who admonishes the nations, does He not discipline? He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge?' God corrects whole nations in history and is the source of all human knowledge. If He can do that, He surely knows what individual wrongdoers are doing, and He can correct them too. The Teacher of humanity is not ignorant.
verses.context: Jeremiah 10:24 prays, 'Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice.' Isaiah 28:26 says God instructs the farmer and teaches him the right way. Job 35:11 says God teaches us more than the beasts of the earth.
explore: Admonish
To warn or reprove firmly, pointing out wrong and urging change.
Discipline
Correction meant to train and improve, not merely to punish.
verses.reflect: What has God taught you through correction in the past?
verses.alt: Farmers listen to an elder beside a freshly plowed field.

verses.title: Futile thoughts
verses.heading: Known by the LORD
verses.meaning: Verse 11 concludes, 'The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile.' God not only sees actions; He reads thoughts. And He knows how empty human schemes are without Him. The plans of the proud are like breath, here and gone. Paul quotes this verse to humble those who boast in human wisdom. Only God's thoughts endure.
verses.context: 1 Corinthians 3:20 quotes, 'The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.' Psalm 139:2 says, 'You understand my thoughts from afar.' Ecclesiastes 1:2 calls life under the sun without God a vapor.
explore: Futile
Empty, worthless or vain, like a breath that vanishes.
Thoughts
Inner reasoning, plans and intentions of the heart, fully known to God.
verses.reflect: Which of your plans need to be handed to God because they feel empty without Him?
verses.alt: Morning mist drifts away from a valley as the sun rises.

verses.title: Blessed by discipline
verses.heading: Taught from Your law
verses.meaning: Verse 12 turns from fools to the faithful: 'Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law.' Correction can feel painful, but here it is called a blessing. God disciplines those He loves, shaping them through His Word. Being taught by God means He has not given up on us. The contrast is clear: fools reject instruction, but the blessed welcome it.
verses.context: Proverbs 3:11-12 says, 'Do not despise the LORD's discipline... for the LORD disciplines the one He loves.' Hebrews 12:10-11 says discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness. Job 5:17 calls the one God corrects blessed.
explore: Blessed
Truly happy and favored by God, enjoying His goodness.
Law
God's instruction, the Torah, teaching His people how to live.
verses.reflect: How might God be lovingly shaping you through something difficult right now?
verses.alt: An elder reads a scroll aloud to a family under an olive tree.

verses.title: Relief from trouble
verses.heading: A pit for the wicked
verses.meaning: Verse 13 explains discipline's purpose: 'to grant him relief from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.' God's teaching gives inner calm while trouble lasts. The faithful can rest even before justice arrives. Meanwhile, the wicked are digging their own ruin. The picture is of a hunter's pit slowly being prepared. Evil's end is coming, and the faithful can wait in peace.
verses.context: Psalm 37:7 urges, 'Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him.' Psalm 7:15 says the wicked dig a pit and fall into it. Matthew 11:28 records Jesus promising rest to the weary.
explore: Relief
Rest, calm or quiet given in the middle of trouble, not only after it.
Pit
A deep hole dug to trap animals, a picture of the downfall awaiting evildoers.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God's rest while you wait for things to be made right?
verses.alt: A traveler sleeps peacefully beside a campfire under bright stars.

verses.title: Never forsaken
verses.heading: His people kept
verses.meaning: Verse 14 gives a firm promise: 'For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage.' Whatever oppressors do, God will not walk away from those who belong to Him. His commitment rests on His own faithfulness, not on how strong His people feel. This truth anchors the whole psalm and comforts all who feel left alone in suffering.
verses.context: 1 Samuel 12:22 says, 'The LORD will not abandon His people for the sake of His great name.' Romans 11:2 says God has not rejected His people whom He foreknew. Hebrews 13:5 promises, 'Never will I leave you.'
explore: Forsake
To leave or abandon someone, especially when they are in need.
Heritage
God's own people, His inheritance and treasured possession.
verses.reflect: When have you felt abandoned, and how does this promise speak to that feeling?
verses.alt: A shepherd carries a lamb back toward the flock across a hillside.

verses.title: Justice restored
verses.heading: The upright follow it
verses.meaning: Verse 15 looks forward: 'Surely judgment will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.' Corrupt courts will not last. One day justice will return to what is right. When that happens, the upright will gladly follow it. God's people long for a world where right is honored, and Scripture promises that the Judge will bring it about completely.
verses.context: Isaiah 9:7 promises the Messiah's kingdom will be upheld with justice and righteousness forever. Amos 5:24 calls for justice to roll on like a river. Revelation 21:5 records God saying, 'Behold, I make all things new.'
explore: Judgment
The decisions of courts and rulers, here returning to fairness and truth.
Upright in heart
Those whose inner motives are honest and aligned with God's will.
verses.reflect: How can you live now in a way that matches the justice God will restore?
verses.alt: Elders sit together fairly hearing a case at a city gate.

verses.title: Who will stand for me?
verses.heading: Looking for a defender
verses.meaning: Verse 16 asks, 'Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Who will stand for me against the workers of iniquity?' The psalmist looks around for someone to defend him and finds no one. It is the lonely feeling of facing injustice without allies. This question sets up the answer in the next verse: when no human stood with him, God did.
verses.context: 2 Timothy 4:16-17 records Paul writing, 'No one stood with me... But the Lord stood by me.' Isaiah 59:16 says God saw there was no one to intervene, so His own arm brought salvation. Psalm 142:4 laments that no one cares for my soul.
explore: Rise up
To stand and take action on someone's behalf, especially as a defender.
Workers of iniquity
Those who make a practice of doing evil and harming others.
verses.reflect: Who has stood up for you in a hard time, and how can you stand for someone else?
verses.alt: A lone figure stands in an empty city square looking around.

verses.title: Unless the LORD helped
verses.heading: Saved from silence
verses.meaning: Verse 17 answers: 'Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence.' The 'abode of silence' means the grave, where no voices are heard. The psalmist was close to death. Looking back, he knows his survival came from God alone. Gratitude grows when we remember how near we came to disaster and who rescued us.
verses.context: Psalm 124:1-2 says, 'If the LORD had not been on our side... when men rose up against us.' Psalm 115:17 says the dead who go down into silence do not praise the LORD. 2 Corinthians 1:10 says God delivered us from deadly peril.
explore: Helper
One who comes to aid; often used of God as the rescuer of His people.
Abode of silence
A poetic name for the grave, where life and speech have ceased.
verses.reflect: Looking back, where can you see that God was your helper when you could not help yourself?
verses.alt: A rescued traveler sits safely on a ledge above a deep gorge.

verses.title: My foot is slipping
verses.heading: Held by loving devotion
verses.meaning: Verse 18 is deeply personal: 'If I say, My foot is slipping, Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me.' At the very moment he admitted he was falling, God's steadfast love caught him. Honest confession of weakness opens the door to help. God does not wait for us to be strong first. His love holds us up exactly when we feel ourselves going down.
verses.context: Psalm 73:2 says, 'My feet had almost slipped.' Deuteronomy 33:27 says, 'Underneath are the everlasting arms.' Matthew 14:30-31 records Peter sinking and Jesus immediately reaching out to catch him.
explore: Slipping
Losing footing and beginning to fall, here a picture of faltering faith or strength.
Supports
Holds up or sustains, keeping someone from falling.
verses.reflect: Where do you feel your foot slipping, and can you say so honestly to God?
verses.alt: A hand grips a climber's wrist on a steep rocky slope.

verses.title: When anxiety overwhelms
verses.heading: Consolation that delights
verses.meaning: Verse 19 says, 'When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul.' The Hebrew pictures many troubling thoughts multiplying inside. Anxiety can crowd the mind until there is no room to breathe. Yet God's comfort does more than calm; it brings delight. His presence can turn a racing mind toward joy. This verse is a gift to anyone who struggles with worry.
verses.context: Philippians 4:6-7 urges, 'Be anxious for nothing,' promising God's peace to guard our hearts. 1 Peter 5:7 says, 'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.' 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 calls God the God of all comfort.
explore: Anxiety
Many troubled, multiplying thoughts and worries that weigh on the mind.
Consolation
Comfort and encouragement that eases distress and restores hope.
verses.reflect: What anxious thoughts can you bring to God right now in exchange for His comfort?
verses.alt: Soft lamplight glows in a quiet room as rain falls outside.

verses.title: A corrupt throne
verses.heading: Mischief by decree
verses.meaning: Verse 20 asks, 'Can a corrupt throne be Your ally, one devising mischief by decree?' Some injustice is official, written into law by rulers who use legal power to harm. The psalmist knows God cannot partner with such a throne. Laws that legalize evil remain evil in God's sight. Authority is meant to serve justice, and God stands against rulers who twist it.
verses.context: Isaiah 10:1 says, 'Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees.' Daniel 6:7-9 describes a decree crafted to trap Daniel. Romans 13:4 says rulers are God's servants for good.
explore: Corrupt throne
A ruling power that has turned to injustice and abuses its authority.
Decree
An official order or law issued by a ruler with legal force.
verses.reflect: How should you respond when laws or leaders around you call evil good?
verses.alt: A scribe seals an official scroll with wax in a dim palace room.

verses.title: Condemning the innocent
verses.heading: Banding together
verses.meaning: Verse 21 describes the plot: 'They band together against the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.' Evildoers unite to give their schemes the look of legitimacy. Innocent people are sentenced through false charges. This pattern reappears throughout Scripture, most clearly in the trial of Jesus, the truly innocent One, condemned by leaders who joined together against Him.
verses.context: 1 Kings 21:13 tells how false witnesses accused Naboth so he was stoned. Matthew 26:59 says the council sought false testimony against Jesus to put Him to death. Acts 4:27 says rulers gathered together against God's holy servant Jesus.
explore: Band together
To join forces as a group, often to accomplish a shared purpose.
Innocent
Free from guilt, not having done the wrong one is accused of.
verses.reflect: How does Jesus' unjust condemnation give hope to those who suffer unfairly?
verses.alt: A crowd gathers outside a courtyard gate under torchlight.

verses.title: My stronghold
verses.heading: Rock of refuge
verses.meaning: Verse 22 is the psalmist's confident response: 'But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge.' After all the injustice described, 'But' turns everything. Corrupt powers may rule for a time, yet he has a safer place. A stronghold is high and walled; a rock of refuge cannot be shaken. His personal 'my God' shows trust built through experience.
verses.context: Psalm 18:2 says, 'The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.' Psalm 62:7 says, 'My mighty rock, my refuge, is God.' Matthew 7:24-25 records Jesus describing a house built on rock that stood firm.
explore: Stronghold
A secure, high, fortified place where one is protected from enemies.
Rock of refuge
A solid rocky place of shelter, picturing God as unshakable protection.
verses.reflect: What helps you turn from looking at injustice to resting in God as your refuge?
verses.alt: A natural rock fortress rises above a wide valley at sunset.

verses.title: Their own iniquity
verses.heading: The final word
verses.meaning: The psalm ends in verse 23: 'He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness. The LORD our God will destroy them.' Evil eventually turns back on those who do it. God lets their own wrongdoing become their ruin. The final repeated line, 'The LORD our God,' shows the psalmist resting in God's ownership of the outcome. Justice is certain in His hands.
verses.context: Proverbs 26:27 says, 'He who digs a pit will fall into it.' Esther 7:10 tells how Haman was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Galatians 6:7 says a man reaps what he sows.
explore: Iniquity
Wickedness or sin, here the guilt that comes back upon the wrongdoer.
Destroy
To bring to complete ruin, here God's final judgment on unrepentant evil.
verses.reflect: How can trusting God with the outcome free you to do good even when wronged?
verses.alt: A collapsed wooden snare lies empty in a field at dawn.
